title: Chapter 20: Boss Level 4: The Tested Quiz App
video_title: Python Chapter 20: Boss Level 4, The Tested Quiz App
summary: New staff at the Corner Cafe keep getting prices and allergens wrong. Follow Asha as she builds a staff quiz from three modules and writes its eight tests before the code. An AI assistant helps at all six stages. Her tests catch its confident mistakes: a rule that cannot be tested, a percentage that gives 0, and a shorter grade that changes one sign.

scenes.title: Acceptance criteria
scenes.direction: Six criteria in groups, a quiz on the pure-rule criterion, then a breather.

visual.heading: Done means all six are true
visual.label: Acceptance criteria
items: The questions live in `quiz_data.py`.
The rules live in `quiz_logic.py`, with no `input()` or `print()`.
Spaces and capitals do not matter. A blank answer is wrong.
A whole-number percentage: 75 or more is Ready, 50 or more is Almost.
The last line looks like `Score: 3/4 (75%) Ready`.
Eight tests, written first, all pass. Four typed runs give known results.

segments.say: Asha writes down what done means.
One and two. The questions live in one module, and the rules in another. No rule asks or prints.
Three. Spaces and capitals do not matter, and a blank answer is wrong.
Four and five. A whole-number percentage, a grade, and a last line like this one.
And six. Eight tests, written first, all pass, and four typed runs give known results.

visual.question: Why must the rule `check_answer()` not call `input()`?
options: It would make the quiz slower
A test cannot type an answer
`input()` only works in the app file
visual.explain: A test calls the rule with fixed values. A rule that waits for typing cannot be tested.

segments.say: Quick check, from Chapter 17. Why must the check answer rule not call input?

after.say: B. A test calls the rule with fixed values. A rule that waits for a person to type cannot be tested.

items: Three files, one job each.
Rules never ask or print.
Eight tests say when it is done.

segments.say: Take a breather. You know the files, and what done means.
Next, Asha plans the functions with an AI assistant.

scenes.title: Plan it with AI
scenes.direction: Stage 1: the AI's plan puts input() inside a rule. Asha checks it against criterion two and replaces it.

messages.text: I am a beginner. I know functions, modules and pytest. I want a staff quiz with four questions, a check for each answer, a percentage and a grade. I will write the tests first. Do not write code. List the functions I need, and the file for each one.

Use three files. In `quiz_logic.py`, write `ask_and_check(question)`: it asks with `input()`, checks the answer and returns True or False.
Also add `percentage()`, `grade()` and `result_line()`.

segments.say: In this project, all six AI stages help build one module: the rules. Stage 1: plan. Asha asks for the functions she needs, and says: no code yet.
The AI suggests three files and four functions. The first one, ask and check, asks the question with input, checks the answer and returns True or False.
Asha checks it against criterion two. Ask and check does two jobs, and one of them waits for a person to type. No test can check it.
So she keeps the three files and the last three functions. She replaces the first one with a pure rule: check answer, given and correct. The app asks. The rule only compares.

scenes.title: Step 2: Tests first
scenes.direction: Walk the test file in groups, teach assert not and the docstring-only stub returning None, then predict how many tests pass. Quiz on test-first.

visual.heading: Step 2: Eight tests, before any rule

segments.say: Step 2 is the big change. Asha writes the tests before any rule exists. The file imports the four rules she plans to write, by name.
Lines 6 and 7: an exact answer is right. Lines 10 and 11: spaces and capitals are still right.
Lines 14 to 19 use assert not. It checks that something is false. A wrong answer and a blank answer must not count.
Lines 22 and 23: three out of four is 75. Lines 26 and 27: two out of three rounds to 67.
Lines 31 to 34 test the edges of each grade: 75 and 74, then 50 and 49.
And line 38 tests the whole last line.
To run the tests, the rules need names. Asha writes each function with only its docstring. No code yet.
A function whose body is only a docstring returns None. Remember: None counts as false.
Now think about the two assert not tests. Not None is True.

ask.question: With these empty rules, how many of the eight tests pass?

after.say: Asha runs pytest, with dash q, dash dash t b equals no, and dash r f.

visual.heading: The first run: no code yet

segments.say: Two pass. Six fail, as expected, because there is no code. The wrong-answer and blank-answer tests pass already, because not None is True.
A test that says this must be false is weak on its own. The exact-answer test is its partner, and it fails until the rule works.

visual.question: You write the tests first. What should most of them do before any code exists?
visual.explain: With no code, a test that checks real behaviour fails. It passes only when the code is right.

segments.say: Quick check. You write the tests first. What should most of them do before any code exists?

after.say: C. Fail. A test that checks real behaviour fails until the code is right. That failure is the starting line.

scenes.title: Step 3: The first rule
scenes.direction: Asha writes check_answer herself, predicts the run, then stage 2: the AI's version, compared on four answers. Breather.

segments.say: Step 3. Asha writes the first rule herself.
Line 7: strip removes the spaces around the answer, and lower removes the capitals. The correct answer gets lower too, so the data may use capitals.

ask.question: With this rule done, which tests pass now?

visual.heading: The second run: one rule done

segments.say: The four answer tests pass. The first four characters of the report are dots.
The four rules without code still fail. One step at a time, the dots replace the F's.

messages.text: Write a function check_answer(given, correct) that returns True when the answer matches, ignoring spaces and capitals. Show only the function.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha wrote her rule first. Now she asks the AI for its own version, without showing hers.
The AI calls lower before strip. A different order. Does it matter?

visual.heading: Her version and the AI's, side by side

segments.say: Asha runs both on the same four answers. Line 10 holds the answers.
Exclamation mark r in line 11 prints each answer with its quotation marks, so you can see the spaces and the empty answer.
Every row matches: True, True, False, False. Both versions agree, so she keeps her own.

items: Tests first: six failed, two passed.
`not None` is True, so pair weak tests.
One rule done, four tests pass.

segments.say: Breather. Relax your shoulders. One rule is done, and the tests say so.
Next, Asha lets the AI write the other three rules.

scenes.title: Step 4: Let the tests judge the AI
scenes.direction: Stage 3: the AI's percentage rule and its promise; the learner predicts percentage(3, 4). Stage 4: the run, three failures, the shared function. Stage 5: the report, the cause, the fix, all eight again. Quiz, breather.

visual.heading: Generate: code that must pass my tests

messages.text: Here are my eight tests. check_answer() is done. Write percentage(), grade() and result_line() so that all eight pass. Do not change my tests.
Here is the percentage rule. The other two follow the grades in your tests. This module passes all eight of your tests.

segments.say: Step 4. Stage 3: generate. Asha pastes her tests and asks for the other three rules. Do not change my tests.
The AI writes the module, and says: this passes all eight of your tests. It sounds sure.
Look at line 12. Remember floor division from Chapter 2: the double slash keeps only the whole part.

ask.question: With the AI's line 12, what does `percentage(3, 4)` return?

after.say: 0. Three double slash four is 0, and 0 times 100 is still 0. The AI's promise is wrong. Asha runs the tests to be sure.

visual.heading: Stage 4, Test: her tests run the AI's module

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha runs her eight tests on the AI's module. The first four dots are her own rule. Then F, F, a dot, and F.
Three tests fail: three of four, percentage rounds, and result line.

visual.heading: Test: which rule do the failures share?

messages.text: I ran my eight tests on your module. Three failed: test_three_of_four, test_percentage_rounds and test_result_line. Which function do they have in common? Do not fix anything yet.
All three failing tests call `percentage()`. Two test it directly, and `result_line()` uses it for the score.

segments.say: She asks the AI what the three failing tests have in common, and says: do not fix anything yet.
All three call percentage. Two test it directly, and result line uses it for the score.

visual.heading: Stage 5: one failing test, in detail

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha runs one failing test with the details on, using dash dash t b equals short from Chapter 19.
The report shows the test line, and the real value: 0, not 75.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: The report says percentage(3, 4) gives 0. First explain why. Then show the smallest fix. Do not change the test.

`//` is floor division. 3 // 4 is 0, and 0 times 100 is still 0.
The fix: divide with `/` first, and round at the end.

segments.say: She pastes the report and asks for the cause first, then the smallest fix.
The AI explains the double slash. Its fix divides with a single slash first, and rounds at the end. One line changes.
Asha does not run only the test that failed. She runs all eight again.
Eight dots. Eight passed. The AI sounded sure the first time. The tests were the only thing that knew.

visual.question: You fix one rule. Which tests do you run next?
visual.explain: A fix can break something else. Run every test after every change.

segments.say: Quick check. You fix one rule. Which tests do you run next?

after.say: D. All of them. A small fix can break something else, and only a full run shows it.

items: The AI said all eight pass. Three failed.
`//` gave 0 for 3 out of 4.
After the fix, all eight ran again.

segments.say: Breather. The rules are finished, and every test passes.
Now, the app that does the talking.

scenes.title: Test it
scenes.direction: Four typed runs with expected last lines, a prediction on spaces and capitals, the blank run as proof, then the results table.

segments.say: The rules pass their tests. Now Asha tests the whole app. Each run is a copy of the app with its own typed answers, and a last line she knows in advance.
Full marks, which you predicted.
Zero. Three for the tea is close to 3.50, but it is not the same text, so it is wrong.
Spaces and capitals.
And four blank answers.
The spaces and capitals run. For the cake, the barista types CARROT in capitals, with spaces around it.

ask.question: Does `"  CARROT "` count as a right answer?

after.say: Yes. Strip removes the spaces, and lower removes the capitals. Correct! All four count: 100 percent. Pass.

segments.say: Four blank answers. Each one gets the right answer printed, and the score is 0. No crash. Pass.
Here are the results. Every real last line matches what Asha expected.
All four runs pass, and so do the eight tests.

scenes.title: Improve it with AI
scenes.direction: Stage 6: a shorter grade() that changes one sign. Ask what grade(75) returns, then the test run. Six stages table, breather.

messages.text: Every test passes. Make grade() shorter. Do not change what it returns.
Drop `elif` and `else`. `return` already stops the function, so the next line runs only when the first check is false.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Every test passes. Asha asks the AI to make grade shorter, and says: do not change what it returns.
The AI says: drop elif and else, because return already stops the function. That idea is correct.
Here is the AI's shorter version. Read line 17 carefully, and compare it with Asha's rule: 75 or more is Ready.

ask.question: With the AI's version, what does `grade(75)` return?

after.say: Almost. Line 17 says greater than 75, not greater than or equal. The AI changed one sign.

segments.say: Asha runs her tests. Two fail: the grade boundaries, and the last line, which now says Almost.
Line 31, the boundary test from step 2, found it in less than a second. Asha keeps her own grade.
